client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. I can't seem to focus at work at all — I'll be in the middle of a task and suddenly just feel this wave of sadness hit me out of nowhere. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help, honestly, because nothing is going to bring her back.
therapist: I'm so sorry for the loss of your grandmother — what you're feeling makes complete sense, and those unexpected waves of grief can be truly disorienting, especially when you're trying to function at work. You're right that nothing will bring her back, and I want you to know I'm not here to fix that or take the pain away, but simply to sit with you in it and help you find ways to carry it. I'm curious — when you think about your grandmother right now, what's one memory or feeling that comes up most strongly for you?

client: When I think about her right now, the first thing that hits me is this image of her kitchen — the smell of whatever she was always cooking, and how she'd just talk to me like I actually made sense, you know? It's weird because I feel guilty too, like I didn't call her enough in the last year, I kept telling myself I'd visit and then I just... didn't. That guilt is almost worse than the sadness itself.
therapist: That image of her kitchen and feeling truly *seen* by her — that's such a beautiful and tender thing to carry with you, and it speaks to how meaningful your bond really was. The guilt you're describing is incredibly common in grief, but I'd gently invite you to notice that the very fact you're hurting this much is itself evidence of how much you loved her. I wonder — do you think she knew she was loved by you, even during that last busy year?

client: I want to say yes, I think she knew... but then I immediately second-guess myself, because what if she didn't? Like, I told myself she understood I was busy, that she knew I cared, but I never actually said it out loud enough during that last year, and now I can't go back and fix that. The idea that my love for her is somehow visible in how much I'm hurting right now is a nice thought, but it doesn't really quiet that voice in my head that says I should have done more.
therapist: That voice telling you that you "should have done more" is worth examining gently — it's speaking with such certainty, but it's also only telling you one side of the story, leaving out years of love, presence, and connection that your grandmother experienced from you. Guilt often tricks us into believing that loving someone *more* would have looked different, but the fact that you *knew* she'd understand your busyness suggests she'd already shown you who she was — someone who saw you clearly and loved you anyway. What do you think she would actually say to you right now, if she could hear that voice in your head?

client: I've thought about that question before, actually, and part of me knows she'd probably tell me to stop being so hard on myself. But there's this other part that wonders if I'm just... making that up because it's what I want to hear, you know? Like, maybe I'm using her kindness as an excuse to let myself off the hook too easily.
therapist: That's a really honest and self-aware observation — you're essentially questioning your own comfort, which shows how seriously you take your responsibility to her. But I'd gently ask: is it possible that someone who made you feel like you "actually made sense" really *would* respond to you with that same grace, and that recognizing that isn't letting yourself off the hook, but rather *receiving* the love she already gave you? What would it feel like to allow yourself to accept her kindness, even now?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, but it almost feels like I'd be using her kindness as a way to excuse myself. Like, she was generous with me, and if I just lean into that, I'm taking advantage of her goodness rather than actually sitting with the weight of what I did. It's hard to separate "accepting her love" from "letting myself off too easy."
therapist: There's something really meaningful in what you just said — you want to *honor* the weight of this, not just dissolve it away, and that impulse actually speaks to your integrity rather than your guilt. But I wonder if there's a middle path here: one where you can hold both the genuine regret *and* her love at the same time, without one canceling the other out — because sitting with grief and accepting love aren't actually opposites. What would it look like for you to acknowledge the regret without it becoming a punishment you feel you have to carry indefinitely?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that's possible — holding the regret and her love at the same time without one wiping out the other. But honestly, it feels almost too neat, like a nice idea that doesn't quite land in reality when I'm lying awake at 3am thinking about all the visits I didn't make, all the phone calls I put off. How do I actually do that in practice, not just as a concept?
therapist: That 3am experience is so real and raw, and you're absolutely right to push back on anything that feels like just a tidy concept — what you need is something that actually meets you in those dark, restless moments. One small thing that some people find helpful is, in those moments, to try writing down one specific, concrete memory of something you *did* give her — not to erase the regret, but to make sure your mind isn't only presenting you with one kind of evidence. What do you think would happen if, alongside the missed visits, you also let yourself name one thing you genuinely gave her during her life?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to try it, but I'm honestly worried that whatever I come up with will just feel hollow compared to the weight of what I didn't do. Like, I made her a birthday cake one year, or I called her on Sunday mornings for a while — but at 3am my brain immediately goes, "yeah, but then you stopped, didn't you." I'm not sure I trust myself to hold onto the good memory without it getting swallowed up by everything else.
therapist: Your brain at 3am sounds like a relentless prosecutor that only admits certain evidence — and it's worth noticing that those Sunday morning calls *happened*, they were real, she received them, and no amount of later busyness can actually unmake them. The fact that things faded doesn't erase what came before, even if your mind keeps trying to argue otherwise. I'm wondering — when you imagine your grandmother hearing you describe those Sunday calls as something small and hollow, what do you think her reaction would actually look like?

client: I think she'd probably laugh a little and tell me I was being ridiculous, honestly. She always did that when I was too hard on myself, kind of a gentle "oh, stop it" sort of thing. But then I immediately think, well, that's just what she would have said to make me feel better, so maybe it doesn't actually count as real evidence either.
therapist: It's striking that you just described her so vividly and specifically — the little laugh, the "oh, stop it" — that's not something you invented just now, that's a real memory of who she actually was with you. And I'd gently point out that you're now dismissing *her* character as evidence, which means the bar for what "counts" keeps moving in a way that makes it impossible for anything to offer you relief. What would it mean for you if her consistent kindness toward you was simply... true, and not a trick she was playing to let you off the hook?

client: I hear what you're saying, and yeah, I can't really argue that I made up that laugh or the way she used to wave me off when I complimented her cooking. But if I let myself believe her kindness was just... real, just true, then I have to sit with the fact that I pulled away from her in those last couple of years, and she was still like that with me anyway. That feels worse somehow, not better, like it makes what I did even harder to justify.
therapist: What you just touched on is actually something really profound — you're not avoiding the pain anymore, you're moving closer to its real center, which is that she loved you generously even when you weren't showing up the way you wished you had. That's not evidence that you're a bad grandchild; it's evidence that she knew you more completely than your worst moments, and chose you anyway — and grief that feels *that* specific and tender is often where the deepest healing quietly begins. I'm wondering — is it possible that what feels unbearable right now isn't really guilt about what you did, but the ache of realizing how much she gave you that you can no longer give back to her?

client: That actually... yeah, that lands somewhere really deep. Like there's this weight I've been carrying that I kept calling guilt, but maybe it's more like... I had all this love left to give her and now there's nowhere for it to go. And I don't know what to do with that, because it doesn't feel like something that can just be healed — it feels like it'll just sit there forever.
therapist: What you just named - love with nowhere to go - is one of the most honest and beautiful descriptions of grief I've ever heard, and I want you to sit with the fact that you just found that yourself, in this conversation. That love doesn't have to just sit there frozen; sometimes people find ways to let it move — through keeping a small ritual that honors her, cooking something she made, or even just talking about her the way you have today. I'm curious — is there anything in your life right now, even something small, that feels like it could be a place where that love might find some expression?
